newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Cash cocoa buyers scarce but shippers well sold.
newsitem.headline: Cash cocoa buyers scarce but shippers well sold.

text.p: Ivorian shippers offloading cash cocoa at prices beneath the market are now pretty well sold but buyers are thin on the ground, frightened off by the recent speculative price jump, traders in Europe said on Friday.
"Many buyers missed the market on the way up and they are not going to step in now," one trader said. "Everybody is complaining that no one is selling a bean."
"The shippers are pretty well sold, they had very favourable currency movements in the first part of the year," said another.

Traders quoted Ivorian March shipment cocoa at around 25 stg under the May contract and a similar differential was quoted for April/May. New crop was only attracting bids at 35 stg under but there had been hardly any traded, they added.

Ghana, following its recent policy of entering the physical market only on futures rallies, has also been active in the past few days, offering cocoa at differentials little changed from last week's 10 to 15 stg under LIFFE for forward shipments.
But offers have met with few takers as inventories in western Europe seem to be sufficient to satisfy the forward needs of most of the major cocoa consumers.
"Cocoa stocks in Europe have continued to grow and buyers are just not concernced they will run out of cocoa, one said.

The futures market has remained strong this week, with the May contract hitting a near eight-month high of 1,050 stg a tonne on Wednesday. By Friday, prices had eased a little to trade nearer 1,040 stg.

Traders described the move as technically-inspired but some also cited talk of a high proportion of small-sized beans in the upcoming Ivorian mid-crop, which has been subject to drier than normal weather conditions.
"It's possible the dry weather has had an impact and there are stories going around but it's a bit early to say from here," one European trader said.

Others noted recent weather reports of rain in the country's cocoa belt which they said had improved the chances of a good-sized mid-crop, although it is still expected to be well short of last year's bumper 200,000 tonnes.

The futures price spike in which the structure of the market has also tightened and fears over the abundance of Ivorian mid-crop cocoa has again focused attention on what Phibro, the trade house thought to control one third of world stocks, plans to do with its large physical position.
There have been signs the company was looking for long term gains and had no plans to scale down its holdings.
"If they (Phibro) decide to put a squeeze on July or September there will be a lot less cocoa around and that could be interesting," one said.
